utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to everyone. Yes, I can follow in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner assisted by Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm with David Cunningham and Aleksandar Vujic this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Preliminaries, and there is one matter that I will deal with, but I'm waiting for some photocopies to be done and I want to deal with it in private session. I think we need to wait a couple of minutes until the photocopies are ready, because I also have to give them to my two colleagues. Nothing special, Ms. Korner, so it's not a big problem. It's something that more or less concerns Mr. Ackerman more than the rest of us. So that's number one. Number two: You were supposed to come back with feedback on your motion, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm here to backfeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Basically what I have to tell you is that I am willing to accept your offer. I propose that we begin on 14 October rather than 13, but other than that, your offer is acceptable. So we would start on the 14th of October with the two witnesses that are to be cross-examined, and then go from there straight into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- beginning to call Defence witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go through this bit by bit. And that means basically instead of finishing the Defence case -- you will finish the Defence case one week earlier than the date I mentioned last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understood that was the offer, Your Honour, and that's what I've accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the position, you've got more support on my right, Mr. Ackerman. But that doesn't save you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, consult your left. Maybe the two of them will ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's go through this. We are agreed that for most intents and purposes, Prosecution case will be concluded, save for what I will be saying, on the 1st of August. Then it's the understanding that in the week, last week of August, I understand that there was some discussions yesterday between one member of my staff with you, Mr. Cunningham, and with -- someone -- that's what I am informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to bring that up. We're suggesting that we sit during that week on the Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, which would be I think the 29th, 30th, and 31st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am told as follows: I will not mention names because I am not quite sure whether they are protected witnesses or not. I spoke this afternoon with Mr. Cunningham regarding the schedule of Prosecution witnesses for the last week of August. Currently, there are two scheduled to appear. The first is BT19, who is scheduled to appear on Thursday, 28th, and Friday, 29th of August. That's agreed and that stands as it is; correct? (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's right. And there's one to come back for cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the second witness is the one you've just referred to who is scheduled to return for cross-examination, if ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If ... Your Honour, he would be on the Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm told -- Mr. Cunningham asked whether the Chamber was planning on calling this person on Monday, the 25th, which would likely result in a break between that witness's testimony and BT19. He expressed a clear preference to start on Tuesday, 26th, or perhaps Wednesday, 27th. He has spoken to Ms. Korner who was apparently in agreement. This is what I'm told.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is what -- Your Honour, unless I was dreaming, I don't recall having any conversation with any legal officer on this subject yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I thought Your Honours were saying -- certainly I spoke with Mr. Cunningham about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So you agree that, if possible, we'll try to get that witness on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wednesday the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's -- it is also agreed already between the Chamber and Mr. Ackerman, in particular, that following the testimony of these two witnesses, you will have an additional time for the filing of a supplemental Rule 98 bis addendum. Shall we leave it open until when we need to cross the bridge, so that you practically or more or less know how much time you would require, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I suppose so, Your Honour. There's even a significant possibility that I won't require any time at all to file the supplement. It may not be necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So it is understood also that these two days remain firm, August 22nd being the deadline for the Defence filing of the Rule 98 bis motion, and September 5th being the deadline for the Prosecution 98 bis response.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the only other thing I'd ask is if before we break on Friday, Your Honour were to set dates first of all as to if the case continues, obviously, for when Mr. Ackerman must supply us with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The list of witnesses, yes, yes, yes. I'm coming to that. I'm coming to that. Because it's -- I was planning on the assumption that we would give Mr. Ackerman this extra week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the assumption that he would agree with our offer, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we plan to hand down our oral decision on the Rule 98 bis as planned, that is, on the 3rd of October, on the 3rd of October. In view of this, we have set the 29th of September as the date, final date by which you, Mr. Ackerman, need to file whatever you require to file under Rule 65 ter (G). All right? Then on the 3rd of October, following our decision on the Rule 98 bis, we will have the pre-Defence conference. So the filings of the list of witnesses, et cetera, needs to be done on the 29th, Mr. Ackerman. On the 3rd of October, we hand down Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. our decision. We hope. We have agreed yesterday on a very tight timetable during which we hope to be able to reach -- cover all the territory of the Rule 98 bis and hand down an oral decision. That should enable us then to hold a pre-Defence conference, on the same day. That's the idea. The opening of Defence will be then on the 14th, on the Defence case, will be on the 14th of December -- of October. And I haven't got the last ... I will tell the registrar, then, or my legal officer, the date when you're supposed to close your defence. We should now be in a position to issue a comprehensive Scheduling Order covering also the closing and the rest. All right? Okay. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the subject of -- just quickly on the subject of witnesses, because we had the same problem in Stakic. It is absolutely vital that we are provided not only with the name of the witness, but the date of birth and the father's name. Otherwise there are so many people, as Your Honours know, with virtually the same name, in order for us to properly conduct our researches. We do need that information. And this was a problem that became very acute in Stakic. So can I just mention that now so it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Ms. Korner. And Mr. Ackerman, please take note of that. So we can bring the witness in. No. The other thing I wanted to tell you -- let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. Ackerman, and I thank you for your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Judge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's cut it short. Please proceed with the solemn declaration and we will try and finish with your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge. Please take a chair. And Mr. Cunningham will continue with his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If we could show the witness Exhibit P22, please. Cross-examined by Mr. Cunningham: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the exhibit that we left off with yesterday, a document, a telex, delivered to, it appears, the -- at least in this case it was delivered to not your municipality but another municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday I think you told us that the document had Mr. Brdjanin's signature on it. In fact, it does not have his signature on it. It doesn't bear anyone's signature; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It bears no signature. What I meant was is that there was the name, as if it was signed. Normally you wouldn't be able to have a document like this signed. It's a difference in terminology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I want to talk about -- there were 14 directives listed in this telex, and I want to go through them quickly. I think you told us yesterday that with respect to number 1, at no time was a military command of the town ever formed in your municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although there was a significant amount of pressure from the military to do that; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was round-the-clock duty in your municipality for about a week and if memory serves me correct in your statement you said that no one really wanted to do that, so you disregarded the around-the-clock directive after a week; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Cunningham, because we have a problem, at least two of us. It seems that in our records there is some confusion between P23 and P22. I have the right P22, but we need the exhibit to be put on the ELMO so that the three Judges can follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so there's no confusion in anybody's mind, it is actually the telex allegedly signed by Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely. And I remember in the first weeks of the trial that this -- we had problems with this document, actually. Yes. My apologies to you, Mr. Cunningham, for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to number 2, which deals with establishing the full mobility of the TO, this was never carried out, and I believe in your testimony from last Thursday, you testified it was not within the municipality's authority to carry out full mobilisation; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That is not within the authorisation of the municipality, but we had no need to do this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a third directive there that says form units for the front and designate their replacements. And in your statement at page 16 of the English statement you said that this was not done, and you even went so far as to call this portion of the order a stupid order. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph number 4, directive number 4, specifies that all men under the age of 40 are to be reassigned from civil protection to the TO, and the TO is to be resubordinated to the corps as wartime units. Again, this was not something within the authority of your municipality to do; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no authority for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 5 talks about a directive to take over the management and public enterprises, the post office, SDK, bank, judiciary, and by all means the media. It was impossible for your municipality to do this; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't physically impossible, but it was unnecessary, superfluous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, and I apologise for not having the page number, I believe you said the following, and I'm quoting you: "In our town, in our municipality, only two managers were changed, were dismissed and been replaced or appointment and in this period not a single one, and the only one that was dismissed -- and only one was dismissed, and that was a Serb." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Do you recollect what you were referring to there?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I do need the page number for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me go to the next one and I'll come back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the -- directive number 6 had you -- you were ordered to or directed to proclaim a wartime programming schedule on radio stations, and I think on page 16 of your statement you said that that was out of the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You mean the interview or the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The interview. That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true what you've just quoted. These instructions are not -- they do not coincide with our remit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean with "our remit"?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant is that it is possible that it coincided with other areas, other remits, other municipalities. At the time, we only had some citizens of our municipality were mobilised in Lika and Dalmatia front. So there was no need to declare any kind of wartime schedule of the programmes. In contrary to other municipalities that had a large number of citizens mobilised on other fronts, so the situation was completely different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back to number 5. Number 5 says, "Take over management in the public enterprises, the post office, SDK, bank, judiciary and media." And a moment ago I couldn't put my hand on your tape-recorded statement from June 2003. I can now do so. And this is what you said in response to talking about these directives. I'm reading from page 16, line 5 of my copy: "Number 5: Take over authority, power, and public companies, post office. That was impossible. In our town, in our municipality, only two managers were changed in -- were dismissed and been replaced or appointment, and in this period, not a single one, and only one was dismissed, and that one was a Serb." Do you remember -- first of all, do you remember saying that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly how I said it, and I can add that the director of the post office was a Muslim, then of the sawmill, he was a Muslim, and there were some other people. I cannot recall all of them, and you know why. And during that period, nobody was fired. No director was replaced. It was only at the end of 1992, in the course of 1993, that one director was replaced, who was unable to organise the production as requested, and he was a Serb. And the head mistress of the secondary school was appointed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So it sounds like, to me, that within the industry in your municipality, within -- the people that would fall underneath the public enterprises, post office, SDK, bank, judiciary, and media, you did not have the sort of dismissals of Muslims that you did in other enterprises; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no firings in other companies. There was no firings like this. As I stated yesterday, it started in the spring and summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let's move on with the further discussion of this telex. Let's talk about number 7. Number 7 is calling a meeting of the directors, agreeing on the means of supplying the populace with everything from electricity to consumer goods. Prior to the date of this telex, your municipality was already doing that; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to this telex, our municipality, yes, was doing these things concerning the supplies, because there was a shortage of certain things and a surplus of others. So we were trading during this period of time and after the telex. That is, this telex did not affect our business relations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the remainder of the items listed on this telex, numbers 8 through 14, those were not implemented in your municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. I remember that there was some building going on even during the war. When I said that many of these instructions were nonsense, I meant that lots of things were unnecessary or simply redundant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned lots of construction going on in your municipality. Your president even was involved in some construction during the war period; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The president of the Executive Board. They were building -- they were constructing a building next to the municipal hall. I know that he was building a business premises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at number 12. "Paramilitary formations, if they exist, to be disbanded immediately and reassigned to the Territorial Defence. This must be carried out without fail." You see that, don't you? Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When it talks about paramilitary formations, it's not merely talking about Muslims, is it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: How I read this, it refers to Serb paramilitary formations, because it is notorious -- it is common knowledge that there were paramilitary units in some municipalities which went, as a rule, to the front in Croatia. We had regular mobilisations for the front, and I must say that people are not particularly keen on responding. And at the time when there was effectively good and firm authority, people who would attempt to form paramilitary formations would have been arrested, because, as you know, such men, such individuals, are quite reluctant to go to the front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Let me go to another topic now, because I want to talk with you and visit with you about the ARK Crisis Staff and your municipality's relationship with Mr. Brdjanin. You told us in your testimony that when the ARK was proclaimed, it was supposed to adopt all the duties of government. Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how I understood it, basically. The government or the ARK was -- yes, it was expected that it would be formed, and with all the duties that go with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All the duties and obligations that go with governance, including dealing with the economy, schooling, pensions and health plans, paying salaries to governmental employees; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. These duties and obligations in the first place, and other things that governments are supposed to do, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I bring up those four or five things that I just listed for you because in your testimony, your LiveNote testimony from last Friday, at page 34, you told us that the government barely functioned, if at all, in these areas; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct; at least, in our area, we did not see any serious results coming out of that government. We never received any funds from them. We simply did not feel there was any economy going on. I think that even the money to pay the pensions was not coming regularly. And if I remember correctly, I went to Banja Luka to negotiate specifically about that particular point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... with respect to those negotiations; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly that they did pay some of the deferred pensions on that occasion, but to tell you the truth, I don't remember exactly. What I do remember, however, is that that administration worked, functioned, poorly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And because of the poor functioning, you were aware of a number of municipalities, and I believe your municipality petitioned to have Mr. Brdjanin removed as president of the ARK Crisis Staff. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be quite honest, I do not remember it. I saw it in these documents. However, I remember the discontent that existed because of the manner in which ARK functioned. I remember that President Novakovic commented on that repeatedly. I know that he was not happy about it, that when he talked with President Latinovic and Mr. Bilanovic, who was a member of parliament, and they agreed that it was not functioning. And that is why I think that it would be logical for them to request the dismissal. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just ask: Are you referring to the document of the 14th of June, P247, or something separate?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I was going to talk about P1261.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If we could show the witness that exhibit, P1261, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we only got the list this morning. It's not in the Petrovac binder, so I wonder if I could ask for it to be put up on the ELMO. I have no idea what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I repeat again, rather hopelessly, three days before the end of our case, it would be nice to get the list before cross-examination starts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's an exhortation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And it's well taken, Your Honour. I apologise to the Court and counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know that you usually are -- you are extremely careful, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My notes, sir, reflect that this is an exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Can we at least --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- on to the ELMO so we can see what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I understand that. Let the witness read it, and we put, once he's read it, we put the English text on the ELMO for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I believe there's another portion of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is it Prijedor you want the witness to have?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Well, this is one of the exhibits that I can talk about, because this is on my list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at this exhibit, and I know you just read it for the first time, sir, this is an indication from --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Before you go on, Mr. Cunningham, the question was: You put to him that Petrovac had petitioned for the removal of Mr. Brdjanin. The question I asked is: Is that based on the document of the 14th of June, which is Exhibit P249? This is something completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I know, and I'm withdrawing that question and asking him a question about this one now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you're not suggesting there's any document --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: No. I'm not suggesting that this document says that. I plan on returning back to that with the proper exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed with 1261 and see what the question is going to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This question, it appears it's a conclusion by the Prijedor Crisis Staff, signed by their president, or signed by their chairman of the Crisis Staff, which says that they're not accepting and considering ARK Crisis Staff decisions before 22 June to be invalid; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I see these two documents. I wasn't even aware that municipal mayors, municipal presidents, had requested these dismissals so openly and declared such decisions invalid. This is the first time I see this. So that all I can say is that I know from their conversations that they were not happy with the manner in which it functioned. But this is the first time that I learn that they requested these changes so explicitly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this document in front of you would be an indication, at least in Prijedor, that they are not -- that there's some discontent with the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's pure comment. It's not a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes, Ms. Korner. Objection sustained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I guess the tenor of what we've been talking about is: At least within your municipality, your president was not very pleased with the leadership of the ARK Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. There are many questions related to this. So I will add: Traditionally, for reasons that I've explained, we were not linked with Banja Luka, but with Bihac. And after we separated from the Bihac region, we provided the prerequisites for us to function even without any decisions or assistance from Banja Luka. At that period of time, and that is why the discontent in our case was not excessive, and perhaps that is why this was not requested, or at least not as openly as this. And for instance, I do not remember that any of our bodies, of our agencies, dismissed, rejected these decisions and refused to comply with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statements, in your testimony, you have alluded to the fact that you did not believe that Mr. Brdjanin was an effective leader or was -- was an effective leader; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Judging by what came from the ARK and from what I heard from our representatives, I -- yes, I assumed that he was not an efficient leader. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had a personal opinion about his abilities that you expressed in your statements; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Cunningham. Sorry to interrupt you, but your question was whether he believed or not that Mr. Brdjanin was an effective leader, and he's answered that he was not, in his opinion, an efficient leader. The two are not exactly the same. Effective is one thing, efficient is another. You can be completely inefficient but very effective.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question, just to follow up on His Honour's directive, is: There's a difference, as he said, between effective and efficient. Do you believe he was an effective leader? And if you can say so, fine; if you can't, that's okay too.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, efficiency and performance, to my mind, are synonyms; and no, I do not think that he was effective.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your testimony, you've talked about how President Novakovic had numbers for members of the presidency, such as Karadzic and Plavsic, and could pick up the phone and call them on a regular basis. You also referred to the fact that in Exhibit P1870, that President Novakovic had conversation was General Mladic. In your diary, we have seen that there is the number for the Crisis Staff and Mr. Brdjanin. Having said that, I want to ask you some questions. Were you aware of any telephonic contact between President Novakovic and Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether he talked with him, but the numbers of all the institutions, of all the leaders or more prominent figures, he had all their telephone numbers. At times, he tasked us, the secretaries who were there, and requested from us to communicate with individuals. But he also had direct satellite numbers and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever tasked to call Mr. Brdjanin on behalf of your president?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your testimony, you have talked with the Prosecutor's questions, talked about the implementation of certain orders, and I want to read you two passages that you testified to, first on Thursday, then on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Friday. On Thursday, at page 26 of the LiveNote testimony, you testified as follows: "The general principle was to carry out these decisions, and this was done, except in special cases. Where it was impossible to carry them out, when from a technical point of view or legal point of view it was not possible to carry them out, or it was not sensible to, but generally they were respected." And obviously now we're talking about ARK Crisis Staff. You also said the following last Friday, at page 45: "The president urged everybody to respect the decisions, regardless of the persons behind them, whether it has to do with the military or the Krajina, that is, the AR Krajina or the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is, if one thought the decisions were purposeful, they were put through. Only the decisions which made no sense, which served no purpose and did not have anything to do with our area, they were not implemented or could not be implemented, especially those which were quite illegal and could therefore entail grave consequences at a later stage." Do you remember testifying to those passages?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find those pages, but yes, that is what I said. I remember that that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And here's my question: Who decides when a directive or an order serves no purpose in the municipality? Is that a judgement call that you make or the president makes?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that judgement was, as a rule, made by Mr. Novakovic. Of course, prior to that, he would seek other people's advice I mean, depending on the nature of the decision, he would consult with his associates and other members, representatives of administration. But as a rule, he was the one who decided what would be implemented and what wouldn't. That was according to what I could see regarding those decisions, and that was the only logical way, because the decisions were pretty general, and what was applicable to another municipality or area was not applicable in our case, or vice versa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any general written -- let me rephrase that. Were you aware of any written standards kept in your municipality, or any other municipality, for deciding if an order made no sense, served no purpose, or did not apply to the area?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no written standards. Under the then circumstances, one simply couldn't do any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It sounds like, to me, then, the decision whether to implement or not was largely an ad hoc decision made by the municipality on a case-by-case basis; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to talk to you about the gazettes, because I know with your background in administrative law, and law, that those are important documents, important periodicals for those involved in law; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the time period that you were at Petrovac, there were problems not only with the form of the gazettes, but your receipt in that municipality of those gazettes; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, tape-recorded statement, at page 46, you characterise the gazettes as shoddy and careless, and also stated you did not even know where the press was; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the word I used was nonsensical, or absurd, and I don't think that a printing house was ever hired. I think they were copied manually. You can see it from the way they look.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And it is these problems with the gazettes, and maybe some others, that prompted you to be tasked with going to the Crisis Staff and raising the questions that you did about the gazettes; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was just bi-activity, sideline activity when I went to Banja Luka once. I was to see people at the technical service and see what was the matter with the Official Gazette, because we were simply not receiving them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And this is what you said in your tape-recorded statement at page 85: "Some of the decisions were delivered to us, and some of the gazettes, but some weren't. It depended. Sometimes when people would come back from the meetings, they would bring decisions if they had been finished, or gazettes, and sometimes they wouldn't, and it was a little -- it was a little difficult to implement these decisions if we didn't know the full content and we had to [Realtime transcript read in error "no"] implement." Correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So a problem in trying to get matters implemented was you didn't have what was supposed to be implemented in the form of a gazette or other directive; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to talk to you with Exhibit P25. If we could show you that exhibit. This document is the instructions for the organisation and activity of organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina in extraordinary circumstances, Main Board SDS, 19 December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think line -- page 23, line 20, just for the record, this was your question, Mr. Cunningham, but I don't think it is reproduced correctly in the transcript. Was a little difficult to implement these decisions if we didn't know the full content and we had no implement. "The full content of what we had to implement." That's how it should read. Then he, of course, answered: Yes, yes, it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're acquainted with this document having seen it in your interview and in your testimony; correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I want to go over some of these instructions to you. One of the instructions under Variant A, number 2, was: Provide conditions for daily meetings of the secretariat and order to continuously monitor and assess the situation on the ground. In your municipality, you did that at first, even though the order said daily meetings, after a while you did not have daily meetings; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And basically, I think you said at your tape-recorded statement the reason that that happened is no one really wanted to do it, so it only lasted a week or less. That's what you said at page 29 of your statement. Does that sound right?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In here, you were supposed to send reports back to the ARK Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was -- was that your duty to send those reports to the ARK Crisis Staff, or was it Mr. Sikman's?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, formally, that was Mr. Sikman's duty, but frequently I was tasked with compiling this in writing and preparing it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And obviously, you can vouch for the work you did, but are you in a position to vouch in light of Mr. Sikman's other obligations, that he got his reports to the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that he sent the reports, but these were not his reports; these were reports that in fact the president sent, and he always verified. He had to be shown what had been written.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. One of the directives, directive number 4, is to convene and proclaim an assembly of Serbian people in the municipalities. No assembly of the Serbian people of Bosanski Petrovac was ever declared, was it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because this was not referring to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And I think if we were to look at number 5, your answer would be the same. This was not implemented because you read this directive only applying to those municipalities, such as Bihac or Krupa, that were dividing.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 6 deals with the increase of security at critical facilities. That wasn't done at all the critical facilities within your municipality, was it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, for a few days there was security ensured of a special plant of the waterworks company, and I think that in one company where there was a lot of inflammable material, there was an intensified, internal control, but it was their own security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the control -- or the increased security at the main waterworks, I believe from your statement, you even stood guard out there one night; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was during the day. I did. I did go to stand guard, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, much like the directive that you have daily meetings, after a while, the standing guard over the waterworks fell by the wayside, am I correct, and wasn't done?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 8 talks about -- I apologise. Paragraph number 10 talks about carrying out preparations, creating the organisational means and other necessary conditions. And then under 3 subsets it provides a listing of certain points. That was not implemented in your municipality, was it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, apart from the use of annual leave, some people did, some people didn't. Personally, neither before nor after have I used my annual leave but the rest, going abroad, nobody even wanted to go. There were no requests, so there were no prohibitions. I don't know whether it would have been implemented had there been requests. But as far as annual leaves are concerned, that was because of general circumstances, of a lot of pressure on all the services, all the managers. They mostly did not use their annual leave during the wartime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at number 8, it says, "Intensify information and propaganda activities." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't really have the means for that. That was not done. And in our municipal area, there was no need for that. We only had one radio station that could be only heard in about halfway of the area of a small town. So really, any kind of propaganda to be dissipated by means of a radio, that wouldn't have been effective. What was done was through meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so the decision there on your municipal basis was, based on our circumstances here in Bosanski Petrovac, we are not going to implement number 8 because it just doesn't apply to us; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No decision was made. What was done is that it was done -- it went without saying, through inertia. Simply, it was going without saying. Nobody said anything. For instance, I was present when they said at a meeting the waterworks shouldn't be secured any more, and that was that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me talk finally about number 11, where it talks about carrying out preparations for three or four different subparts. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see item number 11, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your -- I believe in your testimony, and correct me if I'm wrong, you told us that this was not implemented in your municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not. I believe I have given you the reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to talk to you now -- I'm done with that exhibit, if you'd like to hand it back to the usher, please. The next exhibit I'm going to visit with you about is Exhibit P153, which deals with mobilisation. For the record, this is a document dated 16 April 1992, from the national defence minister, dealing with mobilisation; correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was an order for mobilisation that came after the fact that mobilisation had been completed in your municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your testimony from last Friday, at page 46, you said that it came from a source that was simply not acceptable. What were you referring to when you said that the source was simply not acceptable?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the source of the decision?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I have a page number of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: It's at page 46.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry. Page 46 of last Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me phrase it this way, sir. Did you consider the source of this order to be unacceptable?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't recall exactly why I had said that this was unacceptable. In fact, I think I remember I didn't mean to say that the source was unacceptable but that the legal basis was. I think this was a legal basis that has been imaginary one, and I think pursuant to Rule 71, I had said to the chef de cabinet of Mr. Karadzic to Mr. Dmicic, I said that this was playing with legal basis when they had proclaimed the state of war in part of the territory, because this Rule 71 did not give any basis for such authorisation. And that is why such legal document was legally unacceptable. In fact, they had imagined a legal basis. It was a fictitious legal basis and it was produced as being a legal basis for authorising such decisions. It was only later, in 1995, I believe, that they changed it, or perhaps in 1996, when they changed the constitution and when they included the authorisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record -- just for the record, Mr. Cunningham, he's referring to Article 71. In the document -- on the exhibit which I have as P153, there's reference to Article 68 and Article 81, but I don't see a reference to Article 71. Perhaps the witness would like to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps it was a matter of interpretation, or perhaps I didn't state it clearly. But I did mean Article 81. Yes, 81, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Judge. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although there was purportedly a directive for you to mobilise, your municipality to mobilise, your municipality had done that well before the directive came through; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember that your president responded to the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that it was, out of courtesy, although had this Crisis Staff been functioning properly, or had Mr. Subotic's ministry been functioning, they would have had to know that all this has been implemented and carried out perfectly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to follow up when you said that the response was done as a courtesy. In your tape-recorded interview at page 48 you were asked the following question: "Whatever Novakovic's personal opinion of Mr. Brdjanin may have been, he clearly did feel that he had to respond to this request for detailed information?" This was your answer: "Now that I am actually thinking and interpreting this, I think I will be able to tell the truth. I don't think he felt that he had to. I think he wanted to express his solidarity with the others." When you were asked who the others were, you stated: "The other municipalities." Do you remember that testimony or that statement that you gave to the OTP in this area?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that, and that's what I meant this time as well, except perhaps I had done it in a shortened way. When I see this document, this has been signed by Mr. Bogdan Subotic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- okay. I'm done with that exhibit. I'd like to visit with you about Exhibit P153.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 153? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 153 is the exhibit that you've just been using.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: For the life of me, I'm totally unable to find the quote that Mr. Cunningham attributed to the witness saying about this document. He says it's on page 46 of the LiveNote. It's not on page 46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 48, he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And 48 of his written statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 48 of his written statement. That's different, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course it is different.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I don't think he said that about the document. That's why I'm trying to find this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Well, that's why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 48 of the interview I would say, not the written statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I think she is referring to a couple of questions back where I referred to page 46. Ms. Korner then said she had difficulty finding it. I then effectively withdrew that question and asked him flat out did he consider this to be unacceptable and if so, why?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, Your Honour, I'm sorry. That is why, because these things have been asserted like something has been asserted earlier. If an assertion is going to be made, I want, please, to be directed to the page on which it actually appears, and any document that is going to be put to support that assertion. I'm sorry. This is getting --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And that is why, Your Honour, when she made that claim, I withdrew that question and asked a non-leading question to see how he would characterise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, let's proceed and we'll react according to what the circumstances arise -- will be from time to time. But if possible, and actually, it is desirable, Mr. Cunningham, that if you are referring the witness to a particular statement that he may according to you have made, then perhaps you can quote chapter and verse, if not read out to him the relevant part of his statement or of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I'll be glad to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that will help. That will help the Chamber as well, because since we shift from one courtroom to another, here we have the transcript of yesterday's sitting but, for example, but we don't have the transcript of last Friday's, because last Friday we were sitting in another courtroom. So that creates problems for us, and if you can more or less stick to what I have suggested, we will find your cooperation extremely helpful. So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You should have Exhibit P157 in front of you, which is an excerpt, and it is signed by the prime minister, 26 April 1992. Do you have that in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd just like to point to the fact that I did not have the document even a moment ago that you were mentioning. I had a document signed by Mr. Bogdan Subotic, who was the minister of national defence of the Serb Republic of BH. So a moment ago I did not have the document that we were discussing, but I just didn't have the opportunity to say so. But now I'll have a look at this following document. But when we were discussing earlier I did not have the right document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I found the passage. I think the confusion arose it had nothing to do with the exhibit that was shown to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- the witness. He said in general terms, general mobilisation, but never referred to P153 so it's wrong to suggest that's what he was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let's make sure that we have the same document. I don't want any confusion. I want to make sure that you have the opportunity to fully and fairly read that document before I ask you any questions about it. Is this a document dated 26 April 1992, Prime Minister Branko Djeric?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your duties in the municipality, did you ever see this document?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever -- do you recall what -- and I don't want you to go through this one by one and discuss them, but generally speaking, look at the documents and determine what, if any, of these 14 points were carried out in your municipality.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to look at all those? Can you tell us which, if any, of those were put into effect in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of these items, for the most part, some of them fully, were implemented in our municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk now about Exhibit 186, please. And I'm done with that exhibit. If we could see a new one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps we could -- usher, we could put the English version on the ELMO, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is from the ARK Crisis Staff, directed to the presidents of the -- to the president of the Municipal Assembly, 11 May 1992. And in effect, what this is, is a statement of account directing that each municipality pay a sum of money on a per capita basis; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the time of this order, the inflation was very, very high. It was, as you said in your statement, at page 39, inflation was unbelievable. Does that sound correct to you?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the economy was also affected by the fact that the mobilisation that we've talked about caused the production in factories to be suspended because workers were in the military; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your -- you, in your position, you were not responsible for the payment of the money listed here. That would be another agency or entity within the municipal government; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe your testimony here was that you assumed that this had been paid; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at page 39 of your statement, you said the following, and I want to see if you can resolve what I see as the contradiction. You were asked about this very same document, and you said as follows, starting at line 7: "No, at least I don't remember, but this Autonomous Region had to be financed somehow, so I -- I believe it had to be financed somehow. I remember the payments were made, but the inflation was unbelievable at the time. There -- there was chaos, so that may have been the reason why payments were not made." In that paragraph that I just read to you from page 39 of your statement, at one point you say "I believe that they were made," and then you say: "That may have been the reason why payments were not made." Do you have any documents to show -- are you aware of any documents showing that these payments were actually made?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In both cases, I stated this on the basis of my recollection of general circumstances at the time. I know that the municipality, in relation to all the partners, they always paid everything on a regular basis, and that's why I said I believe that they were. I have no exact knowledge, because that is the administrative -- or rather, the general administration, the financial department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a lawyer and as a judge, don't you think the best evidence of the implementation of this would be documents from that agency showing the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. payment rather than your mere assumption that it was paid?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course that is so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me talk to you now about the disarmament of paramilitary groups within your municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I'm done with that exhibit, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: This is a good point to break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly, because I was going to ask you whether you envisage to finish this part in two minutes. So we'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we took our break, sir, we were about to launch into a discussion about the paramilitaries that were in Bosanski Petrovac, and I want to focus in on that time period, say, from mid-July 1992 through the end of the year. Mid-July on, there was a problem with what I called yesterday renegade soldiers in your municipality committing crimes against person and property; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was a subject of great concern to your municipality doing something to stop the damage; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I showed you earlier a document, P-22, which was from the president -- excuse me. It was from the order of the SDS in Sarajevo, talking about the disarming of paramilitaries, and you remember that notation; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your municipality ever able to take effective steps to disarm Serbian paramilitaries that were in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you misunderstood me. These were not paramilitary units from Serbia. Some of them perhaps passing through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just talk about the ones that you would characterise as Serbian paramilitaries passing through. Were you able, as a municipality, ever to implement a system that effectively disarmed these, what I'll call, Serbian paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't, but once again -- well, yes. No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to talk to you about the dismissal of non-Serbs from positions within the municipality. Now, obviously this was a subject of debate within your municipality because there were many on the -- many in the Crisis Staff, many in government, who believed that these individuals, these Muslims, were responsible workers who did their jobs effectively and efficiently; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And much like in other areas, the primary pressure on you, you being the Crisis Staff, you being municipal government, to dismiss the people came from the military; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't to dismiss people who came from the military, but the pressure was brought to bear by the army to dismiss those officials and clerks who were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a problem in translation and it was due to the poor questioned that I asked, and I think we can agree, and I'll make this point and move on. It was the military who was pressuring the municipal government to sack, to get rid of the Muslims in government; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, its members, members of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And effectively, the army had a spokesperson on the Bosanski Petrovac Crisis Staff, and that was - and I apologise for my translation - Mr. Vrzina; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wasn't its spokesman. That's not what he was. He was the representative. I think that in the army he was the chief of staff of the brigade, that is, Mr. Vrzina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in Crisis Staff meetings, he would, although not the designated spokesman, as the representative, he would always put forth the position of the military on various issues facing the municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. He always presented the views, even though he was not a spokesman. He was the chief of staff, and it was in that capacity that he would take the floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that capacity, when he talked about Muslims in government, Muslims in the economy, he could be counted on to take the position that they should be sacked, that they should not be allowed to continue working; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this pressure created a dilemma within the municipality because there could really be no legal way to sack or dismiss these employees; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as one of the president's legal advisors, you advised him that to dismiss these workers would expose the municipality to liability in the future; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so ultimately, the decision was made to not dismiss them, but basically give them leave without pay that would freeze their jobs so they could get their jobs back, that their seniority would remain and their years of service would remain; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, it was envisaged that everybody would return back to their jobs when the situation calmed down, regardless of their years of service, because they were not fired. There were no legal grounds to do that. So that in principle, even their salaries should be paid retroactively for the whole period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. The Crisis Staff didn't force the companies in the area to sack Muslim workers, did they?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision was -- the companies were served with a decision, but we just informed the companies about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you inform the companies that -- of this option, that is, leave without pay and suggesting to them that they use their own discretion?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, you didn't have such discretionary right. We sent them the original decisions, the source decision of the ARK Krajina, and they wanted us to take a decision and send it to them. And we refused to do that because we wouldn't -- we didn't want to assume the responsibility. We want the managers to assume that responsibility. We decided that we would be held accountable for people -- for our employees if -- I mean, if that matter arose, but we didn't want to assume that responsibility for everybody else. And I remember how my boss on one occasion, when asked by a large company about it, instructed me how to put together the official answer to their query, and I did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While we're talking about the dismissal of non-Serbs, let me just ask you this question, because it's related: Is it true that Serb workers were sacked if they failed to sign -- excuse me, that Serb workers were sacked if they failed to sign a loyalty oath in Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, one didn't have to sign any loyalty. As a matter of fact, I think that two female clerks, two female employees who were Serbs were dismissed. I remember one. I remember even which job she had. But they were dismissed if their husbands, that is, if their family members did not respond to the mobilisation, and that was the test of loyalty. It wasn't that you had to sign something, but if somebody failed to respond to the call-up or if a member of one's family failed to respond to the call-up to join the military service, that was the criterion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me change topics on you because I want to talk about resettlement of the Muslim population and what you have characterised as a temporary property exchange involving the Muslims. Effectively, the large-scale resettlement of the Muslim population in Bosanski Petrovac occurred after mid-July 1992; is that true? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the steps taken by the municipality to transfer property temporarily for protection, that was taken -- those steps were taken after mid-July 1992 as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we talk about the resettlement of the Muslim population within Bosanski Petrovac, was that done with the goal of protecting them or with the goal of eliminating them from your municipality?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was only for protection. I believe it has become clear by now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about the transfer of properties. You talked about -- by the way, you were on the moving-out commission; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first -- it was during my interview with the investigators, and that I learnt about it for the first time, because the commission did not formally sit at the time when I was designated, when I was appointed to this commission, I was on the front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How could it be that you could be named to a municipal commission and not know about it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's possible. I was a lawyer who covered a general area, so I did all sorts of things. And when I was absent, I suppose one of the municipal officials, the president, I guess, put up my name for that commission because there is no doubt that there had to be a lawyer in that commission. And there was a large number of legal problems that cropped up in all these matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm certainly not doubting your qualifications to sit on such a commission, but don't you find it odd that 12 years after the fact is when you are first notified that you are on this commission and it comes during an interview with a Prosecutor? Did you find that odd?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in principle, no, not really odd, because many things were done along the way and purely formally, but functionally I was involved in these matters. The president would assign specific tasks to me. And I was present at all the meetings where these problems were discussed. And I suppose, I assume that since I was there anyway, that there was no need for them to tell me about the decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the municipality devised this programme to transfer the property, the goal was, as I said earlier, and as you have said, for a temporary transfer of the property to the municipality so the municipality in turn could take the steps to preserve and protect the property; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The municipality even went and took the steps of sealing up homes, property belonging to Muslims, to further the goal of protecting and preserving that property; true?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it is in September of 1992 where there is an unfortunate escalation of violence against the Muslim population in your community; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, and I apologise, because I don't have the specific Crisis Staff -- municipal Crisis Staff document in front of me, but do you recall whether your Crisis Staff adopted the position that it would be best that the Muslim population remain in Petrovac? Originally, that was the position adopted; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, despite the position, the public position adopted by the Bosanski Petrovac Crisis Staff, there was an incident where members of the Crisis Staff itself were involved in the secret transfer of prominent Bosnian -- Bosniak representatives; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it happened long before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It happened at a time when the Crisis Staff had taken the position that the Muslim population should remain in Petrovac; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the one hand, you have the public position of the Muslims should remain in Petrovac, and then you have two members of the Crisis Staff, Mr. Milanovic and Mr. Ivanovic, helping Muslims escape from the municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Getting back to September, what had precipitated the spike, the escalation in the violence against the Muslims in September was the death of some Serbian soldiers from Petrovac at the front; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: People -- the Serbian population was very, very upset about the loss of life of soldiers from their own municipality; true?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a result of that, the violence that you've recounted that we've heard from other witnesses occurred. Now, let me ask you this, and I know the answer to this and it's stating the obvious. Your municipality, your organs of authority were not successful in reining in, in stopping this violence; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked yesterday, I believe it was yesterday, about the incident involving Mr. Balic. And just for the record, he is a Muslim; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is, yes. Mr. Balic is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at this time, in 1992, there was a great deal of public discussion about ensuring that the Muslim population was disarmed; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, yes, that too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, secretly, surreptitiously, municipal government or someone in municipal government provided Mr. Balic with a Kalashnikov in order to protect himself; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was done by the police, and I learnt about that only after he died, from a friend of mine who was the public prosecutor, and it was an informal conversation when I found it -- this about. I don't think that other members of the municipal administration were aware of it either; at least, not all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree with me that that would seem to be directly contrary to purported orders directing people to disarm the Muslim population; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the angle that you look at it from. On the surface of it, it is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to talk with you about Exhibit P1878.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And if we could show that to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe this is a document that you reviewed yesterday, and one that we have called -- I think it's from the Bosanski Petrovac -- we call it the ex-pat's club. But this is a letter that you saw outlining the crimes against the persons and property in Bosanski Petrovac, and you said yesterday that certain details were not quite accurately presented, but not deliberately, but simply because they didn't know the facts. Certain details are not quite accurate. When you said that yesterday at page 14, line 21, generally speaking, what were you talking about that the facts were in the quite -- certain details were not quite accurate?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the facts, just bare facts, they are accurate. But when I said that not all was quite true, I meant the killing of the Balic family, which I think is not mentioned here. And I meant that the abduction of that little girl is not mentioned here, because basically, they were Muslims who they thought were disloyal as Muslims. And Mr. Balic was given a weapon because he had publicly stated that he would be a loyal citizen of any government because he simply couldn't care less about that type of government and that was why the police thought that perhaps he might be attacked by Muslims themselves.
