So that is what I meant when I said that it wasn't quite accurate. But the facts, such as they are, yes, they are accurate. These are the incidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we're done with that exhibit. If we could show Exhibit P1849, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 1849. And just to help orient you, sir, Exhibit P1849 is a document that gives a one-sided version of the events when you confronted the citizens at Karanovac in September. And in that document, Mr. Gacesa writes the following: "We also wish to remark that Jovo Radojko, although in our assessment he is a very honest and worthy man, often lacks tact towards citizens and police employees, due to which he has had problems before with the police, having to intervene in order to get him out of trouble." And I understand that this is one side of the story, but do you have any idea what the author of this letter is referring to when he says that you have had "problems before with the police, having to intervene in order to get him out of trouble"?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I clash with the police on a number of occasions, but the gist of the conflict was when I was appointed chair of the commission for the spoils of war. Because the looted property was seized by force in our municipality, and pursuant to the then decree on the spoils of war, on the booty, which was carried by the Official Gazette in 1992, of the then Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, this property could be used only under very specific rules, as there was no room to store it, keep it, things that were bulky, that is, vehicles and other bulky property, was kept within the police station compound, and the police themselves stole that property, and I was responsible for it. So on one occasion the chief of -- the police commander's brother drove 12 tractors away, nobody knows where, and I was held accountable for that. So at a meeting of the Crisis Staff, or rather, on several occasions, I even submitted my resignation in writing, and they always refused to accept it. But then I always said that nobody else could have stolen this but the police, because it was their yard, it was right under their windows. And then they proclaimed me their enemy. And there were other incidents like that which had to do with what they did or omitted to do, because they were not worried about what I said at meetings, but basically because the same positions would then be upheld by the municipal officials. And another occasion, another such instance, it was -- I had been barely appointed to the job and it was sometime in 1991, when the plebiscite of the Serb people was held. The president, Novakovic, then, in order to transport all these commissions and electoral committees and all that, he had provided a tanker of fuel, and it was then distributed on the basis of very specific lists. It was distributed to neighbourhood communities, to different parts of the town, and on that occasion he sent me to a petrol station, that was in the afternoon, after the working hours, to merely check whether the lists were being complied with. So I entered the petrol pump, that is, the room there, but there were lots of people who were very dissatisfied and were requesting that they be given petrol privately. Since we were in the Serb municipality and the refinery in Brod was controlled by the Croats and they were refusing to deliver the fuel and Ina in Zagreb also had failed to supply fuel for months at a time, so that it was in very short supply at the time, so that the president requested rigorous control. And I entered the premises of the petrol pump, at the petrol station, and four Muslims there --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I apologise for the interruption. Just yes or no: The police had a problem with the way that you were -- I take it that the police had a problem with the way that you distributed the petrol, and that was also a cause of conflict between you and the police; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise --

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's that several citizens -- it's that several citizens on that occasion wanted to force me to sign authorisation for them, and there was pushing and shoving in that throng. And then the policeman simply pulled me out of this crowd and sent me on my way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It sounds like you had conflicts with the police because you were trying to do your job and follow the law and apply the law, and they didn't like that; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. I was responsible for these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just let me take you, very briefly, back to the -- your appointment to the chair of the commission for the spoils of war. You did your best, I take it, to preserve that property so that at the appropriate time it could be returned to the rightful owner; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment - I have to be frank, because I have to speak the truth - there was no possibility that was debated as to the property being returned to the owners, but the property was mostly not from the territory of our municipality. But that property had to be registered, listed, according to their technical and technological characteristics, and then only after the war, possibly the owners could be looking for compensation. Because obviously, what is used during the war, it is possible that it cannot be returned as such, full and unscathed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What I'd like to do is take you back to September of 1992, to the events around the third week of September of 1992. I'm going to visit with you briefly about that. Then I want to go over, briefly, some Petrovac Crisis Staff meetings. If you could show the witness, please, Exhibit P1850, 1850, please. This is the press release by your president, asking people to refrain from the unnecessary shooting, uncontrolled waste of ammunition and destruction of goods; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That is the announcement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is the municipal response to the escalating violence that's going on in Petrovac the third week of September of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was an intense escalation of violence that could no longer be controlled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't your president do something more meaningful than issue a seven, eight-line directive to the local radio station? Why didn't he do anything more?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my statement, I have already said that a lot more has been done than that. But there were no results. For instance, there was a special or a separate unit that was established, the Territorial Defence unit, comprising over a hundred people. These were more prominent men, people about whom we knew very well, for sure, that they wouldn't be looting, that they wouldn't be attacking anybody. In order to protect the Muslim population further, their members patrolled, and they were armed. They patrolled in the areas where the Muslims lived. After that, also the reserve police force was fully mobilised, and they tried everything. But the commander of the Territorial Defence, he probably came that morning, because the -- all those unfortunate incidents were going on for three days. He came and he told the president: Replace me, because I cannot do anything. And he told about an event that happened the night before and said that they were helpless, that they had to either start a war among the Serbs or that they would have to be replaced, that he didn't know what to do. He said that his patrol that night had been attacked from an ambush and that they were told, basically, that the people who had ambushed them told them that they knew who they were and that they would kill their families if they tried to do anything. Those people who had been looting were shouting these things to the patrol from the dark, while they were targeting them. And that is when and why the president issued this public announcement. I believe that was his motive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to take you to the meeting of the Crisis Staff that happened very, very shortly before the convoy left, the convoy that you accompanied, I believe, on September 24th, and I think there are notes that are reflected in your diary on this, or the papers that you brought in. Do you know which documents I'm talking about, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. This is to do with the last convoy. Well, I escorted several convoys.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I wanted to talk to you, and if you needed your notes to refresh your recollection, I believe it was at one of these meetings Mr. Vrzina wanted you, the municipality rather than you, to take away money and jewellery from the Muslims to help the war effort, and do you remember him making -- taking that position? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that's what he said. Whether that was officially entered into the minutes, I don't think so, because most of the others rejected such a thing. He spoke in the name of the soldiers, but the soldiers on the front did not know what the main, essential problems were, and they didn't bother with that. They were mostly led by their emotions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And obviously, his view, Mr. Vrzina's view, was not adopted, basically because he was not there at this emergency meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. This was not at all discussed at this meeting, and it wasn't really appropriate. It was the salvation that had to be organised immediately, and I don't think that he was even invited to this meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. Not salvation; rescue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And his, Mr. Vrzina's absence, gave the Crisis Staff, if you will, a way out, because you did not have to deal with that request; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on your prior experience in dealing with Mr. Vrzina and seeing the other members of the Crisis Staff, if his proposition to take away the money and the jewellery from the Muslim population that was leaving to help fund the war effort, if that position had been made in front of the Crisis Staff, do you believe it would have passed?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would not have passed, and it wasn't passed, because before this large convoy, smaller convoys left, and he also brought this out as the protest of the army. He didn't say that it would just be used for defence, but that this would also enable them to buy weapons for their soldiers. So there were two arguments that he brought out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now follow up on a question that was asked you by the President of this Chamber, and I believe it was on page 47, 48, and I think this happened on Thursday. You were asked: "What had -- what would have been the consequence if you had not implemented the decision had they kept all those employees in employment?" And your answer was, at page 47, 48: "Well, there is no doubt that we would have been removed from the places which we held." And then you discussed the mechanisms. You talk about the population bringing pressure to bear. And then you never really got to the second mechanism, or the second device that would have forced you out. Is it true that in addition to the population, it would have been the military that would have forced you out?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's also true. In fact, the army was a larger-scale problem, because the army was made up of citizens, but armed citizens. It wasn't a well-ordered army. It was more like a militia, like a police. It's a special type of All People's Defence, National Defence, and it was quite difficult to discipline these people. But there was an additional problem. These people, had they stayed in their workplaces, their work was already impossible. As clerks, they would have had to deal with the public, and the public was already armed soldiers, armed citizens, and their families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to talk to you briefly, as a follow-up to something that you testified to about with respect to the police, and your testimony in this regard can be found on 24 July 2003 at page 51. You testified that because of the change from Bihac to the Krajina municipality, functions were being transferred from one regional association to another, and as a result of that, your police actually remained without any kind of real control from a regional centre, and it was effectively without a functional administration. Then you go on to say that the police carried out some of the instructions, but not all, except for some key and dubious decisions. What do you mean when you said by "key and dubious decisions"?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall that. I don't have the document. But the police, if I meant that, I'm not sure about what I meant by "key." Perhaps it's the translation. But if I -- regarding dubious decisions, perhaps I meant unlawful decisions. Obviously, the police did not carry out those decisions that were inappropriate to be carried out. That is generally speaking, but I don't know whose decisions exactly. That would depend who these decisions came from. Was that from the ARK or from the municipality or from the ministry?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, in this area I want to take you back to a passage that you have in your tape-recorded statement at page 75. There you were asked if your president ever informed you about a meeting where a joint proposal was put forward to replace Mr. Brdjanin with Mr. Kupresanin as the Crisis Staff president. I'm going to give you your response, and I want to see if you still confirm that. Here's what you told the Office of the Prosecutor in that interview, and I'm quoting: "He did not tell me about these things, but I know that there was general discontent with Brdjanin's work. The decisions that were made under his authority were illegally, technically unimplementable. They were simply -- they simply created more problems. The ARK, as a body, never functioned administratively. I don't remember a single one need of ours, of the Petrovac municipality, met -- met at this regional level and I don't remember any decisions being made for our benefit. It was just a political body." Do you still stand by that position?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then a little bit further on in that passage, you say, in connection with respect to responding to ARK documents: "We tried to compensate for it in various ways, and we managed to --"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was going to read that out in re-examination, but I'd like the question read please as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the full answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the following -- the question by Ms. Korner in the meeting was: "Right. And one of those problems was this it -- was that you had to respond to the orders and directions. They were given when you thought that these were wrong." Your answer was: "Exactly. We tried to compensate for it in various ways and managed to compensate quite a lot. Unfortunately, not fully, because such decisions were published and people would hear about them and talk about them." That's still your position today, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm leaving that topic. I want to close by just asking you some questions about four or five meetings of the Petrovac Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And with the usher's assistance, I'd like to show you P1830, Exhibit P1830.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at these -- the minutes of the 17th session of the Bosanski Petrovac Crisis Staff held on 22 May on the agenda there are three agenda matters that I want to talk to you about, numbers 3, 4, and 5. Number 3 deals with the establishment of a grammar school.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is: Did you ever receive funding from -- for this grammar school?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. I don't know. But I know that we, as the municipality, provided the initial financial means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to number 4, the decision to establish a medical centre in Petrovac, during I take it because of the circumstances in 1991/1992, and during the war, that that did not come to fruition; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not correct. Later on it functioned as a war hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you -- do you have any idea the source of the funding for operating that as a war hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly from our companies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, I want to talk about proposal number 6, to rename the streets and the town. And you told us that there was a Crisis Staff decision to change the name of the town simply to Petrovac, and that was adopted; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that was adopted. But that was not a final decision. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. What it meant, it was an initiative towards the legislative authority. That would be the only one authorised to change the name of the town and streets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that would be the republican assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Likewise, with respect to the effort to change the names of the streets, maybe one or two street names were changed and the rest kind of fell to the side, decisions were not reached on changing other names?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true. I know that two streets had their names changed, but I don't know whether any more street names were changed, because it was a very heated discussion. Many assemblymen wanted their own names they had, and many streets ended up not being changed. I know about only two streets that were changed. One is where the seat of the municipality is. I know that for sure, and how it was changed. And another street leading up to the house of Mr. Novakovic. I don't recall what the old and the new street was, but I do remember about the municipality street, the Marsala Tita Street was renamed St. Sava Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm done with that document and I'd like to move to Exhibit 1833, that's 1833. And for the record, this appears to be the minutes -- or these appear to be the minutes from the 35th session of the Bosanski Petrovac Crisis Staff which was held on 16 June, 1992. If we look under the agenda number 1, we see that there is a notation in the minutes that the military post demanded that measures be taken against the Muslim population, and then there's a discussion about what to do with the Muslim extremists in the community; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the minutes. I only have the list of these persons, about whom the police decided on isolation, and later on for them to be detained at Kozila. But yes, there was a debate. There was such a debate that had taken place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I apologise for giving you the erroneous exhibit. I didn't do that in an attempt to confuse you. It was just an honest mistake on my part. Do you remember that there was a decision made to isolate the Muslims in a well-guarded facility on the outskirts of town? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that decision was taken for them to be isolated in a large private house which even had a kind of production plant, and there was enough room for many people to be there. But I don't know whether they were there and for how long. I know they were detained in Kozila, because I took delegation of the Red Cross to see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any communication between your Crisis Staff and/or your president and the ARK Crisis Staff, seeking ARK Crisis Staff approval for any step that you took in Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that the president asked permission for this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your response, you brought up the Kozila camp. As a member of the Crisis Staff, were you aware of the mistreatment of prisoners, detainees, at that camp at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't understand this to be a camp. This was considered to be detention, that is, prison. There were no premises that could be designated as prison. I also said that it was arbitrarily decided regarding the selection of these persons. Some of the persons were those with whom hidden weapons had been found, and there was a general conviction in that town that people were detained and taken away as a question of their own security, because the tension was so high that they were not safe to be in town. I am not aware -- I was not aware about anything to do with mistreatment, even later, when I was asking questions, because the Red Cross wanted to see the detainees. Around that time they were released. But I do know that later, when Muslims were leaving, the father of this detainee Ferizovic, Fuad Ferizovic, also known as Beli, who is number 15 of this list, his father approached me and said: Do you know, Secretary, that my son had been beaten up in prison? And I said that I was sorry and that I did not know. And then he told me about the details. He did say something to the policeman, and the policeman beat him up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm done with that exhibit. I'd like to talk to you, finally, about Exhibit 1838, which I hope are the minutes of the 43rd session of the Bosanski Petrovac Crisis Staff, held on June 29th, 1992. And I believe that's a document that you've seen before, and let me know when you've looked at it and you feel comfortable enough to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is coming back to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If we look down under the agenda, we see Mr. Vrzina making a statement about the military base. The record reflects, or this document reflects that he said he had heard the military base and all the depots were being transferred to Banja Luka. He was of the view that this was impermissible and that it should not be allowed. You see that on the face of the document; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the conclusion reached is to draft -- is, under number 3, under conclusions, and that is basically to draft a letter of protest and send it to the Supreme Command of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The appeal, if you will, of this movement was not directed to the ARK Crisis Staff, but rather taken directly to the military; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm done with that exhibit. And the very last exhibit I want to go to is the same one I started with today, and that is Exhibit P22. And I'm almost finished with my questions, sir. I'm looking at the very first paragraph, and I just want to confirm with you that this is an order of the SDS in Sarajevo that was made public at a meeting of all the municipal presidents on 26 October 1991 in Banja Luka, at a meeting chaired by Dr. Karadzic. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all I have, sir. Thank you for your answers. I appreciate your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner. I take it that you have re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may -- could you keep that document, P22, please, because you were asked a number of questions about it. Re-examined by Ms. Korner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you go, please, to item number 5, which you say was not put into effect, take over management and public enterprises, the post office, et cetera. Can you now, please, have a look at P1819. Now, that's the meeting of the 26th of December, where you discuss also what can be called the Variant A and B document. But can you go to item number 7. Deputy Dragan Milanovic raised the question of personnel changes in public enterprises. The vote was unanimous to replace the directors of the power supply company and the veterinary station, while support was extended to the director of the post, telegraph, and telegram service. Now, do you think it's possible there that you were complying with item number 5 of the telegram?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Under item 1, I can't find the minutes of the 1st meeting of the party secretariat on the 26th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Have you been given P1819? If you look, please, at item 7 --

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. 7. Yes, that's right. Yes, 7.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just read --

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Correct. I've read it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The question was: Do you think that you were complying in this decision of the 26th of December with the order number 5 of the telex under Brdjanin's signature in October? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just for the record, it does not bear his signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Under his signature, I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that the minutes, or rather, the meeting was convened by Mr. Milanovic, and he chaired it too. I think it was in a logical order, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So is the answer to my question yes?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, can I ask you this, please: The people who were to be replaced --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. This was in the evidence of -- the evidence of the witness who testified on the 22nd of May, and it's at page 16175. 16174.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was the director of the power supply company a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about him. As for the veterinary station, yes, I know that he was a Muslim, or a Bosniak, if you prefer it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Was the director of the post, telegraph, and telegram service a Bosniak married to a Serb?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the wife. I only talked with him once or twice in the street. But it's possible. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember why the directors of the power supply company and the veterinary station had to be replaced in December?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the electric power supply, I can't remember the exact reason. As for the veterinary one, I do remember that, because that man, as a person, interested me more. He was a passionate hunter. He even hunted around my house, and I heard about him from my parents. There were all sorts of personal remarks made at his dress, made about him, that he was short-tempered or something. But I can't remember any specific reason, I mean any reason that related to the office and the performance that was mentioned, such as, for instance, failure to comply with -- to perform one's duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it have anything to do with the fact that both these men were Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While we're still on the subject, please - you can put both those documents back now - you were asked this morning about the directions given to companies in Petrovac about dismissing their Bosniak employees. Could you have, please, now a letter you looked at, I think yesterday or the day before, P2452. It's the letter of the 21st of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's a letter that I signed, I remember it, because I read it here several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know. I just need you to have it, please. This is the one that you signed on behalf of Mr. Latinovic, which was to the SIP company, who had clearly written before, status of the persons of Muslim nationality concerning their work, in connection with your request to resolve the issues of the status of the persons of Muslim nationality, we send you the answer again, which consists of the following. And then you enclose, as you told Mr. Cunningham, the decision of the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff. You've told us you thought it was illegal. Why didn't you say that to the company instead of just sending them the decision?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, precisely because we thought that this procedure -- I mean the instruction, that that was illegal. Mr. Novakovic, and I think I told you while we were still in Banja Luka, I told Mr. Novakovic that it ran against the law and that we shouldn't assume the responsibility for anything like it. And we wanted them to be aware of the decision so that they could decide by themselves whether they would go along with it or not, rather than have us assume the responsibility for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The company was asking you, as the body of authority - I don't mean you personally; you as the Crisis Staff - what they were supposed to do. Why didn't you tell them?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they basically wanted us to decide and then order them to sack the Muslims from their company, among other places, and we refused it, for the reasons that I have already mentioned. And we did not want to say that to them because, as I said, we thought that that instruction was against the law and that it could entail very grave consequences. But perhaps I didn't quite understand what you meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think I'll ask the question one more time. You, as a lawyer, have told us that you believed this instruction was, from the ARK Crisis Staff, was unlawful because people were being removed simply for their nationality, because of their nationality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, and I told the president that was a pure ethnic discrimination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Absolutely. You didn't, however -- I'm sorry. I'll start that question again. You and your president, when you were dealing with people that came under your employ, didn't formally dismiss them; you sent them home without pay. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because otherwise you believed that you might be sued at the end of the war for unlawful dismissal?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then why didn't you tell this company to do what you had been doing, namely, to simply send the employees home rather than outright dismissal, as this order of the Crisis Staff said?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: For two reasons, the first one being because, in principle, they knew what we had done with our employees and they could follow in our steps. And the second reason is that if we issued such an instruction officially, they might have disseminated and then we could possibly suffer consequences for trying to evade those instructions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Absolutely. And that's the truth, isn't it, as you told Mr. Cunningham, that you would be held accountable if you tried to go against the instructions of the Crisis Staff of the region?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The municipal leadership would have been held accountable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to deal with two other topics that was just touched upon. One is disarmament. It was put to you that you couldn't disarm the Serbian paramilitaries, and you corrected that and said that they weren't Serbian paramilitaries. But you, in actual fact -- if you look, please, again at 1833, first of all, please. Mr. Gacesa - we've been through this before - was telling the Crisis Staff what was happening, and this is the list of 40 people. The operation to disarm Muslim paramilitary units and citizens is continuing. The only disarmament that took place in Petrovac was of the Muslims, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that document in Serbian, but what you say is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all right. Don't worry. And if we look again, and perhaps you needn't bother, because we've already looked at it at P1842, the list that was sent of arms that had been seized, most of them were legally owned hunting rifles, and as you've told us already, the Muslims. Now, can you just also have back one of the documents you were asked to look at a moment ago, again please, P1838. Mr. Latinovic was not a member of the army, was he? He was the president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was of the opinion that all Muslims fit for military service should be singled out and imprisoned to ensure the Serbs' personal safety. So he's not talking there about people who possess illegal arms, is he?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what the minutes say. That is true. But I think that what it was about was those people on whom weapons -- but I mean army weapons were found. Because, to begin with, technically it wasn't really feasible, because it would be six or seven hundred people to have there Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. for all the Muslims isolated and put in detention. I mean, it wasn't -- it couldn't be done. And I think simply that this note is not quite right. But we're talking about individuals on -- who were found to own weapons, and it was on the basis on general conviction or belief among the Serbs that they looked or might present a danger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. So that we all understand: Are you saying that these minutes have made a mistake, that Mr. Latinovic wasn't suggesting that all Muslims who were of military age should be locked up, but it actually said that all Muslims who possess illegal arms should be locked up? Because that's -- before you answer, if you look at the conclusion, that repeats that the persons arrested -- a plan should be made to arrest and bring under custody all Muslims fit for military service, not who possess illegal weapons. If you look back, sir, wasn't it the fact that the people who were being locked up were those simply who were of military age?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the conclusion, you have the second part of the sentence, who could be -- who perhaps could do some harm to Serbs. So that was the proposal. But from my personal knowledge, people -- the persons who were detained, at least, that is my assessment. I don't know what official papers from the times say. But to my mind, not all of those who were detained were fit for military service. I remember a man, for instance, who was a cobbler, and he repaired some shoes for me, and he was an elderly man, and I heard that he had been detained. He was released eventually, but nevertheless, yes, he had been detained. And he had his shop not far from the municipal hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your view, as a lawyer, as has been stressed, were these people who were detained entitled to due legal process? And by that, I mean to be charged with an offence, to be tried.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, under the statute they enjoyed all the rights, and that was one of the main problems, and refusals by the chief of the police to act accordingly. He said that he wouldn't accept it because of the tense relations, and there was a danger that it could escalate, but that everybody had to be aware. And he said that explicitly of it, and that he would consult his superiors and that he would set all those men free when the first opportunity presented itself. After he considered the charges. That took a day or two, because there was the legal deadline by which you had to release them, and that was three days at that time, and I remember him saying that clearly to Mr. Novakovic. He said: As for those who were found to possess illegal weapons, yes, there are legal grounds to press charges against them. But in all the other cases where no material evidence was found, I have to let them go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These people were kept in these detention facilities, as you put them, for some months, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was several months, but I'm not sure. My impression is that they were kept there for a shorter period of time. I know that there was a Red Cross delegation from Knin, which came from Knin and requested to visit them and was supposed to go towards the evening, but it was dusk and they were afraid to do that in darkness. So the next day I went there and we got there in the afternoon, the people had already been released from detention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I have a few more questions. That may be an appropriate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I rather feel -- I don't know whether Your Honours do have any questions. I've got about another 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure that we all have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm wondering if it's not better then to just start the next witness tomorrow. We may be able to conclude him completely him in one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: More or less, we're talking of five, two, three, and maybe I have got another five or ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's hardly worth keeping the witness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we may as well start him fresh tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think yesterday you said that you wanted to hand some documents to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. No, no, Your Honour. Yes. We're going to keep -- when he's finished after he's had some lunch we're going to ask him to go through -- we've got schedules for Your Honours and for Mr. Cunningham of the documents he's already authenticated and he's going to go through the other ones when he's finished testifying, and make a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So 25-minutes' break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to deal with some small points that you were asked about. You were asked about the Sokol society, and you said you were a member; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, when he made contact with this organisation, he in fact recommended me as the president, and formally I was the president of that society, not just a member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But in fact, wasn't the president a young doctor or a medical student named Nenad Stevandic?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. For all of the Sokol organisations, he was. Their seat was in Banja Luka and I was supposed to organise the association or the organisation in Petrovac, but I didn't manage that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Next, can I deal with a point that you were asked about in relation to the Crisis Staff meeting in Banja Luka that you attended, the regional Crisis Staff. You were asked about the recording of that meeting. Do you remember telling us in the interview that there was a microphone in front of the speakers? Page 84 of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. As far as I recall, it was recorded, yes. And the microphone, I think, was certainly in front of the chairperson, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, next, and this is at page 48 of yesterday's LiveNote, you were asked about the alignment of Bosanski Petrovac, even after April 1991 it was suggested that it was still aligned more to Bihac than to the -- well, to Banja Luka. Can I ask you just to have a look for a moment, very quickly, please, at Exhibit P61, 61.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's not on my list. It's arisen as a result of cross-examination. If we can just put, please, the English, first page English, onto the ELMO. That's a list of representatives in the Krajina Autonomous Region Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look down at numbers 21 to 25 on the list, these were the representatives from Bosanski Petrovac, one of which was Mr. Latinovic, effectively your boss. Were you aware that he was attending meetings of the Autonomous Region of Krajina Assembly?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that page. I know on one occasion that he attended and that later on he reported on that. I was not certain whether he was a permanent member, but then according to the list he must have been. I know for sure that Mr. Novakovic was and I also said that I thought that Mr. Milanovic as a deputy must have been as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't worry about that. That's all I want to ask on that document, so that can go. Now, you were asked a whole series of questions about the military presence and pressures on you and that of the police, and you agreed with the suggestion that was put to you that the primary obstacle, the overriding obstacle to doing the right thing in the municipal government was the military. That's page 54 of yesterday's LiveNote. You said: "Well, not in fact the command but simply the units that were out of control." If the military was such an obstacle to good government, did you or Mr. -- well, I'm sorry. Did Mr. Novakovic ever think of going to see General Boric, who was in charge of the 2nd Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did go on several occasions. These were very heated discussions, not only at General Boric's, but also at lower-level commands. But these were informal meetings. As far as I know, there were also telephone protests and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But why informal meetings? If you - as you agreed with the suggestion of Mr. Cunningham - were not able to properly run Bosanski Petrovac because of the behaviour of the military, or military units, why didn't you ask for a formal meeting with the general?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that these were informal meetings, I mean from the point of view of our organs. There were no minutes that were taken on our side. And as a rule, to these meetings, our delegation from our municipal functionaries would go to their headquarters, whether they took minutes there, I don't know. We had to go over there. They did not consider the municipal leadership as an equal negotiator. They didn't consider any municipal leadership as an equal partner. There were a lot of problems with that. But these were informal meetings, but not like the meetings of the Crisis Staff, for instance. They did meet over there, as far as I know, at least. I know that these meetings were planned, and people did go to these meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that Mr. Novakovic was a person of influence who could pick up a telephone and directly speak to Mr. Karadzic. Do you know whether Mr. Karadzic -- I'm sorry, whether Mr. Novakovic ever raised this with Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for certain, but out of some of his conversations, I know that he did raise this issue at a meeting which was informal, I listened to deputy Milanovic when he said that General Mladic was a renegade and that he was not talking to Karadzic or to anyone else. I know that there were quite considerable conflicts. By the end of 1994, at a closed meeting, I was present and that's how I saw that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I'm not interested in 1994. You were being asked about 1992. In 1992, if, as you say, nothing could be controlled because the military were out of control, or units were out of control, do you know whether Mr. Novakovic picked up the telephone to speak to Mr. Karadzic so that he could speak to Mladic, with whichever chain of command? And just answer that yes or no, if you can, please.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because the telephone wasn't considered a secure means of communication for such a conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was put to you that the military didn't turn up to the Crisis Staff meetings. It's right, though, isn't it, if we went back through all the records that we've looked at today, there was always a military representative present at those meetings in 1992, with maybe the exception of the one on the 23rd of September?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us about the incident where retired military officers came and offered to set up a military court, and you've told us that one of the problems was that the military were not subject to civilian courts; they had to be tried by a military court. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, that's how it was according to law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then why not, if you had this lawless military in Bosanski Petrovac, accept the offer to set up a military court so that people committing offences, who wore military uniform, could be tried?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was an unlawful request. That kind of military court that they proposed was not lawful. There was a proper military court, which unfortunately wasn't operational. It existed within the Banja Luka Corps, which was competent for everything. It was a different story. They did not wish to process cases. But we, as a municipality, to establish a military court, that was completely unlawful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked about your record of the meeting of the 7th of June and the fact that, according to what you say - that's the 7th of June in Palanka - the matters that were raised in the document were not discussed at the meeting. Mr. Latinovic went through that document, though, didn't he, when he talked to the Crisis Staff about it? And that's P236. Just have that for one moment, P236, which is the meeting of the 9th of June. I'm sorry. Not Mr. Latinovic; Mr. Novakovic. Mr. Novakovic briefed those present on the conclusions adopted by the Autonomous Region Crisis Staff in Banja Luka, subregions of the municipalities forwarded certain proposals to the AR Krajina government for a prompt organisation of the army and regulation of a central services, et cetera, et cetera. So Mr. Novakovic knew what was in that document, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he did know, except that here Mr. Novakovic, speaking about the ARK, while the other thing was a regional meeting of the subregion, of a smaller association of municipalities. I believe that Mr. Latinovic attended the meeting. That's what comes out from the documents. And I think that I only was concentrating on transmitting the message, which was to do with material damage and looting from one commander to the next. So I wasn't active at the meeting, and that's probably why I don't have any notes from then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, you told Mr. Cunningham that, effectively, you implemented those decisions of the regional Crisis Staff which you could and which applied to your municipality. Now, do you have any recollection of any decision of the Crisis Staff that you -- of the regional Crisis Staff that you did not put into effect?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, today, from that list, although that was the list of the SDS, for certain reasons we didn't implement some things. For instance, from the Crisis Staff of the ARK, we didn't implement things to do with the mobilisation, because it had already been implemented, in essence. That had already been done. And also in connection with the dismissals, that we simply bypassed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I want to deal with that in a moment, but you did, in effect, whether you called it a dismissal or leave without pay, as you've already told us, implement the Crisis Staff decision; indeed, you sent a copy of it to the companies?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, I mean, if we just take one example, and could you have, briefly, P227.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you proceed, even with mobilisation, because the witness keeps saying that mobilisation -- they never needed to implement any decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm about to deal with this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are ample exhibits here, or documents here, that keep repeating exactly the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Quite, Your Honour. Can we just take exactly the example I was about to choose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you look, please, at the 4th Gazette, that is the 8th of May meeting. Item number 1, presidents of the National Defence councils are to supply detailed information to the war staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina about mobilisation. And I'm not going to give you the document again, but P1828, you write --

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that. Yes, I remember the document. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 10th of May, President Novakovic, as president of the national Security Council writes, giving that information, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The president's -- item number 3, presidents of the National Defence council are to report to the war staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina about any actions they may have taken in order to disarm paramilitary units. A report is made, isn't it, about that when it happens?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to carry on on that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now, finally, and this is how matters began yesterday, when you were cross-examined by Mr. Cunningham. He put to you something you had said in interview, at the end, I believe it was, that you believed that the authorities in Bosanski Petrovac - this is page 37 of yesterday's LiveNote - did whatever was possible. "The essential goal, the essential intention, was for people to be removed from danger, and unfortunately, if you look at it from the outside, we seem exactly the same, in a way, as the municipalities that organised the persecution of their population and organised their removal." The first question is: Which municipalities were you thinking of?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to name individual municipalities, but in the press, I read on various occasions, especially after the war, and up to an extent in the wartime press, written, printed by refugees. For instance, a paper published by Muslims, refugees from Sanski Most. And they explicitly said there that they had been rounded up and forced out, forced to become refugees. I also learnt about the municipality of Banja Luka, that there were such round-ups. I could see on Belgrade television, and I could hear people make statements how they had been rounded up and how they had even to pay to be allowed to leave and considerable amounts at that. So these are municipalities that I meant, for instance, and you can find a lot of it in the press.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had a lot of contact with the municipality of Prijedor and Dr. Stakic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These contacts that existed happened twice, and I described them in full. The president may have communicated more often, but not at the time when Stakic became the president of the Serb Democratic Party for the subregion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Would you describe Prijedor as one of the municipalities that organised the persecution of the population and their removal?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of the information that I found, as I have described, yes, I believe that Prijedor was one of those municipalities, and after all, it is common knowledge as to what went on in Prijedor. And today, on our television, we often see stories about people expelled, I mean taken from their homes, and so on. But at that time, I didn't know about it because it was all -- nobody spoke about this. There was silence about it. None of the municipal mayors, at least the meeting I was present, you couldn't hear anything about that, even though one heard that Muslims were leaving our municipalities. But simply, whether it was a taboo subject or not, perhaps in those circles who were rather broad when I was, I mean, present there, so they didn't discuss it, but it was never mentioned. People knew that -- that there were people leaving but nobody knew exactly how.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said to Mr. Cunningham, or Mr. Cunningham put to you that some people might draw the conclusion that Petrovac was involved in persecution, in organised removal, for cleansing purposes, but that really wasn't the case. And he said: "I want to see if you agree with that proposition." And you said: "I agree. It wasn't like that. The situation wasn't like that." That's page 37. Can we just go through what happened in Bosanski Petrovac. The Serbs in Bosanski Petrovac armed themselves. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the way that the question was worded, I tried to give a brief answer. But yes, I agree with what you said there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Muslims were disarmed?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Muslims were sent home from work. If you want to draw the distinction, they were sent home without pay rather than being actually dismissed, but in some cases they were actually dismissed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I believe that they were, because it was a legal nicety, and I'm not sure that in various companies they really understood what it meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They handed over their property, and I'm not going to take you to the documents, but on the basis that they were leaving the municipality permanently, they handed their property over to the municipality permanently; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I explained how things were done. But if you put it that way, then yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just outlining the various things you've told us about. Muslims were imprisoned, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the end, in September, every single Muslim, virtually, left the municipality?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for an insignificant number, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm just going to put to you the figures. This is Exhibit P60. I don't want to have to waste time bringing the document to you. But would you accept that in 1991 the official census recorded that there were 3.288 Muslims in Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it to be an accurate figure. Perhaps slightly more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look, please, at P56. These were figures compiled by the SNB in Banja Luka in May of 1993. If you turn to number 20 on the list, you see -- number 10, sorry. Moved out, Muslims, 3.200. Now, sir, you may not have desired personally that to happen, but in actual fact what happened, wasn't it, in Petrovac was ethnic cleansing in the same way as all the other municipalities?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, yes, but I want to clarify, because I see that something is not -- misunderstood. When it comes to Muslims who moved out. On the 23rd of September, Muslims who lived in the village of Bjelaj stayed there, because of a very short deadline, we couldn't organise the transport for them. There was a danger that we might be waylaid, that we might be caught in an ambush.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How many of them in this village in September, 23rd of September? How many of them were left in this village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, all those who lived there, they stayed on, because technically, it was not possible to evacuate them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And when did they leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not remember exactly. They left -- was it the end of 1992 or beginning of 1993? I remember it was a very cold. I escorted that convoy. I was put in charge of escorting it through Croatia and transferred that population to the area of Bihac. But we entered it from the Croatian side. We went through Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Final question is this, sir: You told us twice, I think, already, that you had to implement the regional Crisis Staff decisions even though you didn't agree with them, because otherwise you would have been removed. If you morally didn't agree with the persecution of non-Serbs, why didn't you resign? Why didn't President Novakovic resign?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about Mr. Novakovic. I did not resign because I didn't know where would I go. And at any rate, I would have been mobilised to a unit, and it was quite uncertain if I would survive in that case. And at that time, one couldn't really flee anywhere seriously, because there were checkpoints and controls all over the place, be they of the police or the army. So that was one reason. And another one was the resignation, especially in Mr. Novakovic's case, and on one occasion I believe I told you that I think he thought that the situation would only get worse if he resigned, even though he gave it serious thought. But then he thought about who might take his place, and invariably he concluded that that person would have enjoyed less authority and to resist some of the decisions or behaviors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge, there are a few questions from the Bench. Judge Janu will start. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Yes, I have a few simple questions for you, sir. Looking at your diary, at entry 20th of July, 1992, you don't need that document. I will -- you write: Banja Luka. And you are discussing to ask Rosic about Svabo, the judge, and you end this day with the sentence: To examine defining of Serbian national question. My questions are concerning this issue: Was there any official definition of national -- Serbian national question? Second question is: Were you tasked to work on this definition? Yes, please, you can answer.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no such definition, and therein the rub. This note, such as it is, means that I was instructed to possibly go to a meeting, but not with Rosic, in ARK Krajina. Therefore, if I went to that meeting, to ask whether it had been defined -- to ask whether it was defined, and how. Because that was one of the questions that people on the ground kept asking. As for the answer to your second question, no, I was not -- I wasn't either that important or that qualified to be incorporated in something like that. But there was constantly informal talk about it, and yet nobody defined it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And sir, I'm still with this point. Taking into the consideration your position and your intelligent order where your mind is working, as I could observe it here during your testimony, I'm sure you were being in the position you were, you were defining this question or you were thinking about it. Could you present us with your own definition, what the national Serbian question was?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one of the first indications of separation along ethnic lines began to emerge and when conflict started, I took it to mean, in the first place -- and when I talked with my friends about it - and I must say that my company was mostly made of Croats, because I lived in Zagreb. And there was a lot of dispute as to about what the Serb national question might be, the question -- the territorial question invariably arrived, the partitioning always arose and we couldn't agree on that. But if I were to define it on my then point of view as to what the Serb national question was, then perhaps the best way to put it would be that members of the Serb people should be ensured the rights which are usual. For instance, the Serbs in Croatia, because that was the topic closest to me. I wasn't -- I didn't know which order I would embark later on. And I thought that the form of the cultural autonomy and economic development advocated by the then leadership of the Serb Democratic Party in Croatia whilst Dr. Raskovic was its head, that option was -- I could accept best, to ensure that the functioning and equality in Croatia. Because regardless of all the propaganda, I do not think that it existed. Because, yes, perhaps there was a larger than average number of Serbs in the army or in the police, but nobody mentioned the reasons for it, and those were not attractive jobs. They were rural population and they were coming to the urban environment. Serbs could never get jobs in banks, in large foundations, or other key --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: I think we should be -- we should end with this question, just additional question. You know personally Vuk Draskovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never met him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: No ideas are close to you, or his ideas are close to you?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I don't know. Various occasions Vuk came up with different assertions, but I just don't know. And I understood Dr. Raskovic's, there is no Draskovic, it is Dr. Raskovic and I felt that his ideas were close to me, but he was removed later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: I thought you are talking about Vuk Draskovic. My second question concerns Mr. Novakovic. Could you please provide the Chamber with conditions under which Mr. Novakovic was mobilised. Was it normal in his position to be mobilised? And the same question concerning to you, because you were mobilised unlawfully, as you said, as well. So if you can be very concise, please, because of the time. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'll be concise. Mr. Novakovic was never officially mobilised, but under the pressure of the commands, which -- that is how I see it, who instigated ordinary soldiers. He had to go to visit the combat units and their positions. He had to do it all the time. And that was a much more dangerous business than being a soldier in a trench, because you go there, you have no idea about either your own or the enemy firing positions. And during one such visit, he was ambushed and killed. I was indeed mobilised, but I received summons for it only the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And you said in your testimony that he was killed on our side, on the Serbian side. So did you learn later on some details about his death?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, I was a soldier on that particular position, a few hundred metres away, and he was half dead as they carried him by. I never learned exactly what happened, and I don't think that anyone knows. You know, there are always rumours when a public figure like that perishes, you know. One doesn't know exactly. But officially, it is thought that he was killed by the Muslim -- by Muslims troops. But he wasn't in a position that was his, properly speaking. It happened, I think, in October, or perhaps November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So you personally don't believe that it was the Muslim army who killed him?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just cannot say. I do not know. I say there were rumours that citizens spread rumours. Personally, I do not trust those rumours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Okay. And my last question: Do you recall some names or a single name of Serbian person, civilian, who was killed by -- in Bosanski Petrovac by a Muslim, Muslim extremist? I'm talking about 1991, 1992, of course.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember any such case. I don't think that there was such a case. But I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I have the cooperation of the interpreters and technicians to go on for the next seven to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Not longer than ten minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I thank you so much. Judge Taya will be asking you a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: On page 18 of your interview, you said in sum that you thought Mr. Brdjanin administratively incapable and arrogant character and you also said that appraisal of yours about Brdjanin was drawn from your personal experience meeting with him and also others' negative saying about him. My question is: Among those who said negative things about Brdjanin, were there any members of ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Novakovic, he was dissatisfied with his work, and I think that Mr. Latinovic, Mr. Milanovic, I cannot remember what they said specifically, but it was my impression that they thought that the ARK Crisis Staff did not work properly. Besides, the Official Gazettes, with decisions that they carried, led me to the same impression too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: On page 75 of your interview, you said you knew that there was a general discontent with Brdjanin's work. My question is: Do you know whether or not this general discontent sentiment was common among the members of ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I do not know, but from what our representatives who attended meetings said, they seemed to say that the representatives of other municipalities were dissatisfied too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: What impression did you have about the extent of support which Brdjanin enjoyed from the members of ARK Crisis Staff during 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of what was being said, it was my impression that they were not really supporting him and that he was dismissed at some point. I don't know from which office and moved to which office. But I know there was such talk amongst them, informal though it may have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I have very few questions left, because some of the territory was covered before by Ms. Korner, in particular. Let's go straight to one point that you testified upon. That's what you referred to as renegade militaries, and sometimes also paramilitaries. And you did state at one time that they were sometimes arrested by the police, but then, since they belonged to the military, they were released to the military. Do you know of any proceedings that the military may have instituted against these persons that were referred to the military by the police?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, the army's reaction was very -- or rather, their command reacted very mildly. From what I heard, only a few of those men received disciplinary punishment. But I'm not aware of any criminal charges being brought against any one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In your interview, and also during the cross-examination, you were referred to the Topalovic incident, and you stated, and also testified, that the police chief, Gacesa, at one point was furious and he said that he will never arrest anyone again unless he received orders from Banja Luka. When he referred to orders from Banja Luka, what was he referring to, or who was he referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the Security Services Centre, specifically, and its head, I think, was Mr. Zupljanin, Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. May the witness please be given Exhibits P1807 and P1837. Let's start with the first one. You will have an opportunity to see it now. In Exhibit 1837 -- 1807 is the minutes of the representatives of the Crisis Staff of the Petrovac municipality. Last page, decision numbered 2, ethnic Muslims shall be engaged in the companies and organisations in accordance with the need that is at the request of the companies and organisations which employ them. This request must be based on the needs determined in the agreed plan of war production. Jovica Sepa voted against this decision. Why ethnic Muslims and not every other person?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely because of the pressures that we've talked about, to engage any Muslims anywhere. And when one looked for a way of engaging them, of getting them to work in the companies that they worked before, but now under labour obligation. And this is a specific form of work, of people fit to serve the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I took the impression while you were testifying that when asked about the refusal to take the oath of allegiance, or swear allegiance to Republika Srpska was not a ground for dismissal or laying off or putting employees on unpaid leave. Did I get the right impression? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. There was nothing formal. It was merely on the basis of that, whether somebody had reported to the army command, which one had been summoned to. So this was an informal criterion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please look at Exhibit P1837, which deals with the decision taken by the Petrovac municipality executive committee to lay off on paid -- unpaid leave, leave without pay, a certain Senada Mehdin. And in the part entitled "statement of reasons" does it say that the Crisis Staff decision, whatever, establishes the obligation to remove from positions specified in item 1 of the decision all workers of Muslim and Serbian ethnicity who, to date, have not given their support to the legitimate government and constitution of Republika Srpska and Bosnia and Herzegovina? Do you stand by your previous statement or would you like to comment on this? Very shortly, because we are running out of time.

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Basically, I stand by what I said before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is a document, P1836, dated 23rd of June, 1992 and signed for Rajko Novakovic which inter alia says mixed police, Territorial Defence and military police patrols shall have the right and obligation to apprehend all such persons, persons that are described in the previous paragraph. On or after the 23rd of June, 1992, were you aware of any such mixed patrols?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such patrols existed, and I said it. I said it even today in my testimony. But I will allow -- I mean, it sounded clear to me, but quite possible that others who only read documents understand it. When I mentioned the Territorial Defence, the mobilisation of more prominent citizens who would patrol and protect Muslim houses and streets, so these are the patrols that I meant and that are indicated here. I do not know whether a police, military police patrolled with them, but the civilian police and those men who did it cooperated fully in trying to prevent whatever, I mean killings, violence, looting, and so on and so forth, and the president merely draws the attention to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. My last question, and please give me a very short answer. You referred to -- Ms. Korner first referred to the events in late September when practically all the Muslims left the municipality, and you referred to some of them remaining in the Bjelaj local commune. I would like you to see P1859, which is an order or decision by the president of the Municipal Assembly. After that, practically all the Muslims had left the municipality, with the exception of small local commune, saying the Petrovac public security station is hereby entrusted to increase patrols in areas where a large number of Muslims live, and especially in the Bjelaj local commune and rigorous measures are to be proposed against any person who threatened the Muslim right to peace, life, and work, or rather, they are to be arrested and handed over to judicial authority. Was there any such decision taken and made public prior to October 1992, when there were more, much more Muslims in the municipality than what was left on the 28th of October, a decision in such strong terms?

utterances.speaker: JOVICA RADOJKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not worded like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I thank you, Judge. I know this wasn't easy, because you have been testifying for three days plus. On behalf of the Tribunal, I should like to thank you for having come over to give testimony in this trial. On behalf of everyone present here, I also wish to wish you a safe journey back home, and you will receive all the attention and all the assistance you require to enable you to do this at the earliest possible opportunity. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, does Your Honour want the list now of the documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have kept everyone beyond --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll ask Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And in fact I should like again to enter a declaration of appreciation and thanks to all the staff, particularly the interpreters and the technicians, for overstaying with us, enabling us to finish with this witness. I thank you all, and we will reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
